narrative: Star Vetter automatically finds candidate eclipsing binary stars in data from NASA's TESS satellite and vets them using a multi-stage pipeline. We sample target stars, extract their light curves, apply statistical quality gates, cross-check against six major variable-star catalogs to flag novel candidates, and perform an automated pixel-level contamination check. Our machine learning model - trained on 752 labeled examples - provides a second opinion on candidate quality and outperforms our rule-based baseline. So far we have examined about 0.6% of the survey area, obtaining usable light curves for 3,541 targets and confirming 86 candidates that passed pixel-level vetting. Each confirmed candidate's page documents its orbital period, eclipse depths, and any caveats that arose during processing. The pipeline is transparent and reproducible: every step is automated, every decision is logged, and the results reflect what the light curve alone can tell us about whether an on-target eclipsing signal is real.

faqs.question: What is an eclipsing binary?
faqs.answer: An eclipsing binary is a pair of stars orbiting each other in such an alignment that, from Earth, each star periodically passes in front of the other. When one star blocks the light from its companion, the total brightness of the pair dips in a characteristic way. These dips repeat at regular intervals set by the orbital period. TESS observes these brightness dips with high precision, making eclipsing binaries among the easiest stellar binaries to detect from space.

faqs.question: What is the difference between a 'candidate' and a 'confirmed' result here?
faqs.answer: 'Candidate' means a target that passed our statistical vetting and novelty check - it shows signs of an eclipsing signal and has not been cataloged before. 'Confirmed' means the candidate also passed our automated pixel-level contamination check, which examines whether the signal comes from the target star itself or from a nearby star whose light may have leaked into the photometry. Confirmation here is a technical milestone in our pipeline, not a statement that the candidate is scientifically validated or ready for publication.

faqs.question: What is the machine learning screening score?
faqs.answer: We trained a logistic regression model on 752 hand-labeled examples to predict which candidates are likely to be real eclipsing binaries. The model outperforms our rule-based baseline and is available on each candidate's page as a second opinion. It does not gate which candidates get checked or determine which ones make it into our catalog - all novel candidates proceed through the pixel-level check regardless of the ML score.

faqs.question: How does the pixel-level check work?
faqs.answer: The pixel-level check is a fully automated analysis that examines the spatial distribution of light in the TESS image stamps around the target star during eclipse and out-of-eclipse phases. It tests whether the dip in brightness comes from the target itself or is contaminated by a nearby star. If contamination is detected, the candidate is flagged; otherwise, it passes this stage and is marked confirmed on our site.

faqs.question: What if the period looks aliased?
faqs.answer: We use an odd/even eclipse-depth test: we compare the measured depths of odd-numbered eclipses against even-numbered eclipses in the light curve. If these depths differ significantly, it can indicate that our measured period is actually a multiple or fraction of the true orbital period (a period alias). When we detect this signature, we flag the candidate's page so users are aware of this caveat.

faqs.question: Can I verify the results myself?
faqs.answer: Yes. Each confirmed candidate's page includes its light curve, measured orbital period, eclipse depths, pixel-level vetting result, and cross-match status against known catalogs. You can download the underlying TESS data and perform your own checks. The TESS archive is public, and all the details needed to evaluate our work are provided.

faqs.question: What happens to a candidate after it appears on this site?
faqs.answer: Being listed on Star Vetter is the final step of this pipeline itself. We do not add candidates to official catalogs, submit them for publication, arrange professional follow-up observations, or track what happens to them afterward. Our role is to vet and catalog them; what the broader community does with the results is beyond our scope.
